title: Water logging and drainage
summary: Waterlogging is caused by over-irrigation with inadequate drainage, and the single most useful insight is that leaching without drainage makes salinity worse rather than better — because the water has nowhere to go and simply raises the table further. Learn the saline versus sodic distinction, because their reclamation differs fundamentally: saline soil is leached, sodic soil needs GYPSUM first, since leaching alone would disperse the clay and destroy the soil structure. Conjunctive use is the elegant remedy, addressing cause and need together.

sections.heading: Waterlogging — causes and effects
sections.body:
**Definition.** A soil is **waterlogged** when its **water table rises so close to the surface that the root zone becomes saturated** and crop growth suffers.

> The **critical water table depth** is about **1.5 to 2 m** below ground. Above that, damage begins.

**Causes** — and note that almost every one is a consequence of irrigation itself:

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Over-irrigation** | Water applied beyond the crop's need percolates and raises the table |
| **Seepage from unlined canals** | The largest single contributor in most systems |
| **Inadequate natural drainage** | The recharge has no outlet |
| **Obstruction of natural drainage lines** | Canal and road embankments block the drainage the land relied on |
| **Impervious subsoil layer** | Perches the water table above it |
| Flat topography, low-lying land | No gradient for outflow |
| Heavy rainfall or flooding | Seasonal contribution |
| Rising regional water table | The cumulative effect of a whole irrigation project |

**The obstruction of natural drainage is the one most often overlooked**, and it is a direct engineering failure. A canal or road embankment running across the slope **cuts the natural drainage lines** of the land above it. Unless **cross-drainage works and sluices** are provided, the land upstream of the embankment waterlogs — not from over-irrigation, but because its outlet was blocked by the project meant to improve it.

**Effects of waterlogging:**

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Loss of soil aeration** | Roots need oxygen; a saturated soil has none. **The primary damage** |
| **SALINITY** | Capillary rise brings dissolved salts to the surface, where **evaporation leaves them behind** |
| **Lower soil temperature** | Water has a high specific heat; germination and growth slow |
| **Weed growth** | Water-loving weeds (and reeds) displace the crop |
| **Delayed or impossible cultivation** | The land cannot be worked or entered by machinery |
| **Loss of nitrogen** | Denitrification under anaerobic conditions |
| Disease and pests | Mosquito breeding, root diseases |
| **Reduced yield, eventually abandonment** | The cumulative outcome |

**The salinity link is the mechanism that turns waterlogging from an inconvenience into a permanent loss**, and it is worth setting out step by step:

1. The water table rises into the **capillary fringe** of the root zone.
2. **Capillary action** draws water upward to the surface.
3. That water carries **dissolved salts** from the soil profile and the groundwater.
4. At the surface the water **evaporates** and the **salts remain**.
5. Salts accumulate year after year, since nothing removes them.
6. The soil becomes **saline**, then **sodic**, and finally **barren**.

So waterlogging and salinity are not two problems but **one process with two stages** — which is why drainage is the remedy for both, and why treating the salt without addressing the water table achieves nothing lasting.

sections.heading: Salinity, sodicity and reclamation
sections.body:
**Two distinct problems**, requiring **fundamentally different** treatment. Confusing them is the most consequential error in the subchapter.

| | **SALINE soil** | **SODIC (alkali) soil** |
|---|---|---|
| Problem | **Excess soluble salts** | Excess **exchangeable SODIUM** |
| **EC** (electrical conductivity) | **HIGH** — above 4 dS/m | Low — below 4 dS/m |
| **ESP / SAR** | Low — ESP below 15 | **HIGH** — ESP above 15 |
| **pH** | Below 8.5 | **Above 8.5**, often over 9 |
| **Soil structure** | **Retained** — flocculated, permeable | **DESTROYED** — clay dispersed, impermeable, hard when dry |
| Effect on plants | **Osmotic** — the plant cannot draw water despite its presence ("physiological drought") | **Toxicity** plus **poor aeration and impermeability** |
| Appearance | White crust of salts | Dark surface (dispersed organic matter), hard crust |
| **Reclamation** | **LEACHING** with good water + drainage | **GYPSUM (chemical amendment) FIRST**, then leaching |

**Measurement:**

> **EC** — electrical conductivity of the saturation extract, in **dS/m**; measures **total soluble salts**
> **SAR** = Na⁺ / √[(Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺)/2], all in meq/l; measures the **sodium hazard**
> **ESP** — exchangeable sodium percentage; the proportion of the exchange sites occupied by sodium

**Why sodic soil cannot simply be leached — the key insight.** Sodium ions are **large and singly charged**, so they hold water loosely and do not bind clay particles together. When sodium dominates the exchange sites, the clay **deflocculates (disperses)**: the aggregates break down, the pores clog with dispersed clay, and the soil becomes **almost impermeable**.

Leaching a sodic soil with low-salinity water therefore makes matters **worse**: removing the remaining salts reduces the electrolyte concentration further, which promotes **more dispersion**, and the water cannot pass through the soil at all.

**The remedy must therefore REPLACE the sodium before any leaching:**

> **Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O)** supplies **calcium**, which is **small and doubly charged** and therefore binds clay particles strongly. Calcium **displaces sodium** from the exchange sites; the displaced sodium becomes sodium sulphate in solution, which is then **leached away**. The clay reflocculates, permeability is restored, and leaching becomes possible.

So the sequence for a sodic soil is **gypsum → irrigate → leach → drain**, and the amount of gypsum required is computed from the **exchangeable sodium to be replaced** (the gypsum requirement).

Other amendments: **sulphur or sulphuric acid** (which produce calcium sulphate by reacting with soil lime), **pyrite**, and **organic matter and green manure** (which release acids and improve structure).

**Reclamation of saline soil:**

> **Leaching requirement LR = depth of drainage water / depth of applied water = EC_irrigation / EC_drainage**

**Extra water must be applied beyond the crop's need** to carry the salts below the root zone. But — and this is the essential qualification — **it only works with adequate DRAINAGE**:

> **Leaching without drainage simply raises the water table and makes salinity WORSE.**

The water carrying the salts must have somewhere to go. If it has not, it accumulates, the table rises, capillary action brings the salts back to the surface, and the position at the end of the exercise is worse than at the start. That single point is the most important in the whole subchapter, and it explains why drainage always precedes or accompanies reclamation.

**Other reclamation measures:** **deep ploughing or subsoiling** to break an impermeable layer, **flushing** surface salts with running water, **scraping** the salt crust (of limited value, since the salts below remain), **growing salt-tolerant crops** as an interim measure (barley, cotton, sugarbeet, date palm, and **rice**, whose ponding itself leaches), and **mulching** to reduce evaporation and thus capillary rise.

**Crop tolerance to salinity**, as a practical scale:

| Tolerance | Crops |
|---|---|
| **Tolerant** | Barley, sugarbeet, cotton, date palm |
| **Moderate** | Wheat, maize, rice, sorghum, sunflower |
| **Sensitive** | Beans, most fruit, most vegetables |

Growing a tolerant crop is not reclamation — the salts remain — but it keeps the land productive while drainage and leaching take effect, which may be several seasons.

sections.heading: Drainage — surface and subsurface
sections.body:
**Two kinds, solving two different problems**, and a field commonly needs **both**:

| | **Surface drainage** | **Subsurface drainage** |
|---|---|---|
| Removes | **Excess water from the ground SURFACE** | Lowers the **WATER TABLE** |
| Problem solved | Ponding after rain or over-irrigation | Waterlogging and salinity |
| Form | **Open channels**, graded land, field drains | **Buried perforated pipes**, mole drains, or **tubewells** |
| Designed by | The **rational method** for a design storm | **Hooghoudt's** or Ernst's equation |
| Cost | Lower | Higher |
| Land lost | Yes — the channels occupy land | No |

**Surface drainage** is designed like urban storm drainage: the **drainage coefficient** (the depth of water to be removed per day, typically **5–25 mm/day** for agricultural land) sets the capacity, and the layout follows the natural slope. Components: **field drains** collecting from the land, **collector drains**, and a **main drain** discharging to a natural watercourse. **Land grading and levelling** is itself a surface drainage measure, removing the depressions in which water stands.

**Subsurface (tile) drainage** — the two forms:

| Form | Character |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal drainage** | **Buried perforated pipes** (formerly clay tiles, now corrugated PVC) at 1–2 m depth, laid to a gradient, discharging to a collector. Suits a **shallow** problem and a **stratified** soil |
| **Vertical drainage** | **Tubewells** pumping from the aquifer, lowering the regional table. Suits a **deep permeable** aquifer, and the pumped water can be **used for irrigation** |

**Hooghoudt's equation** gives the drain spacing:

> **S² = (8 K D h)/q + (4 K h²)/q**

where S is the spacing, K the permeability, D the equivalent depth of the layer below the drains, h the height of the water table above the drain level at midspacing, and q the drainage coefficient.

**The important dependence is on K:**

> **Higher permeability → WIDER spacing**

So a **sandy** soil needs far fewer drains than a **clay**, because water reaches each drain from a greater distance. In a heavy clay the required spacing may be so close that horizontal drainage is uneconomical, which is when **mole drains**, **subsoiling**, or vertical drainage are considered instead.

**Drain envelope and filter.** A perforated pipe laid directly in the soil **clogs**, as fines are carried into the perforations and deposit inside. The remedies:

| Provision | Function |
|---|---|
| **Gravel envelope** (graded) | Provides a **transition** from soil to pipe, retaining fines while passing water |
| **Geotextile wrapping** | The modern equivalent, quicker to install |
| Organic envelope (coir, straw) | Traditional, degrades over time |

The **filter criterion** is the same as for any drainage filter: **coarse enough to pass water freely, fine enough to retain the soil**. Omitting the envelope is the commonest cause of subsurface drainage failure, and it is invisible until the system stops working.

**Drain depth and gradient:** depth **1.0 to 2.0 m** (deeper allows wider spacing but costs more to install), gradient **0.1 to 0.5%**, sufficient for a self-cleansing velocity in the pipe. The **outlet** must be **above the water level in the receiving drain**, or the system backs up — and where it cannot be, a **pumped sump** is required.

**Conjunctive use — the elegant remedy:**

> **Pumping groundwater for irrigation simultaneously LOWERS the water table (solving the waterlogging) and SUPPLIES water (meeting the demand).**

It addresses **cause and need together**, using the very water that constitutes the problem. Its further advantages: it makes use of the **canal seepage** that would otherwise be lost, it provides **flexible on-demand supply** to complement the canal's rostered supply, and it requires no drainage outfall.

Its limitations are real: it needs a **usable aquifer** (permeable, and of acceptable water quality — the Terai's arsenic being a genuine constraint), a **reliable power supply**, and **regulation**, since unregulated pumping leads to over-abstraction and a falling table — the opposite problem. It also does nothing where the waterlogging is **perched** above an impermeable layer rather than connected to the aquifer.

**Nepal's context** for this subchapter:

| Region | Problem |
|---|---|
| **Terai** | **Waterlogging** in low-lying areas, aggravated by **embankments and road/rail formations** blocking natural drainage; localised salinity; **arsenic** limiting conjunctive use in places |
| Inner Terai valleys | Poor drainage, seasonal inundation |
| Hills | Waterlogging rare; the drainage problem is **landslide-related** — intercepting hillside water before it destabilises slopes |
| Kathmandu Valley | Urban drainage and a **falling** rather than rising water table, from over-abstraction |

**In Nepal's hills the drainage problem is inverted**, and it is worth noting because it is where a hill engineer actually applies this material: the object is not to lower a water table but to **intercept and lead away hillside water before it infiltrates and triggers a landslide**. That is the function of the **catch water (intercepting) drain** above a road cut, and of the surface drains and sub-horizontal drains used in slope stabilisation — the same principle of drainage, applied to stability rather than to crop growth.

**Anti-waterlogging measures, as a summary:**

| Measure | Addresses |
|---|---|
| **Lining canals** | The largest source of recharge |
| **Adequate cross-drainage and sluices** through embankments | Blocked natural drainage |
| **Surface and subsurface drains** | Removes the water |
| **Conjunctive use** | Lowers the table and supplies water |
| **Rotational supply and proper scheduling** | Prevents over-irrigation at source |
| **Volumetric water charging** | Aligns the farmer's incentive with efficient use |
| Crop and cropping pattern change | Reduces the water applied — e.g. away from continuously ponded rice |
| **Land levelling** | Eliminates over-application to reach high points |

The first and fifth are the **preventive** measures, and they are the ones that matter most: a project designed with lined canals, adequate cross-drainage and a rostered supply may never develop a waterlogging problem, whereas one that does will spend far more on drainage than the prevention would have cost.

formulas.label: Critical water table depth
formulas.expression: about 1.5 to 2 m below ground level
formulas.note: Above this, root aeration is lost and capillary rise begins to concentrate salts at the surface.

formulas.label: Saline versus sodic soil
formulas.expression: Saline: EC > 4 dS/m, ESP < 15, pH < 8.5, structure RETAINED. Sodic: EC < 4, ESP > 15, pH > 8.5, structure DESTROYED.
formulas.note: Saline soil is leached; sodic soil needs GYPSUM FIRST, or leaching disperses the clay further.

formulas.label: Sodium adsorption ratio
formulas.note: Measures the sodium hazard. Calcium is small and doubly charged, so it binds clay; sodium disperses it.

formulas.label: Leaching requirement
formulas.expression: LR = depth of drainage water / depth of applied water = EC_irrigation / EC_drainage
formulas.note: Works ONLY with adequate drainage — leaching without drainage raises the table and worsens salinity.

formulas.label: Hooghoudt's drain spacing
formulas.note: Higher permeability K allows WIDER spacing — a sandy soil needs far fewer drains than a clay.

formulas.label: Drainage coefficient
formulas.expression: typically 5 to 25 mm per day for agricultural land
formulas.note: The depth of water to be removed daily; sets the capacity of both surface and subsurface systems.

formulas.label: Subsurface drain geometry
formulas.expression: depth 1.0–2.0 m ; gradient 0.1–0.5% ; gravel or geotextile envelope essential
formulas.note: Omitting the envelope is the commonest cause of failure, and it is invisible until the system stops working.

formulas.label: Conjunctive use
formulas.expression: Pumping groundwater lowers the water table AND supplies irrigation water
formulas.note: Addresses cause and need together, and recovers the canal seepage that would otherwise be lost.
